outcomes.absoluteFailure:
Popular tales in Gondor sometimes describe Wargs as beasts of war bred in the secret kennels of the Orcs. These great wolves are said to have been selected since the first conflicts against the kingdoms of Men, then trained to serve as mounts for the warriors of the mountains. Their size and aggression would be the result of generations of breeding, during which the Orcs kept the strongest animals and destroyed the weakest. Wargs are thus presented as a race of domesticated predators, whose hunting habits have been replaced by obedience to their masters. Soldiers' stories sometimes compare them with warhorses, with the difference that their training rests upon cruelty and fear.

Certain traditions claim that Wargs recognise the signs of military authority and lose their nerve before troops arranged according to the customs of the kingdoms of Men. Horn-calls, close ranks, and unfurled banners are said to inspire in them a dread inherited from the defeats suffered by their former masters. The stories maintain that a pack rapidly abandons a pursuit when it encounters soldiers in formation, even if they are few in number. Men familiar with this explanation attribute the danger of Wargs to their speed and their use against isolated travellers, but believe that regular troops can scatter them through a mere display of discipline.
outcomes.failure:
The traditions of Gondorian garrisons tell of the great wolves that accompany certain Orcish forces. These animals are of considerable size, very swift, and possessed of an endurance that enables them to sustain long pursuits. Military accounts describe them as auxiliaries employed to scout the paths, recover fugitives, and harry the flanks of a force. Some can carry an Orcish rider, while others accompany warriors on foot. Their presence is chiefly known from testimony concerning northern regions and territories close to the mountains where the Orcs establish their lairs.

You also know a tradition according to which Wargs constitute a military force wholly subject to Orcish chieftains. Their concerted movements would result from rigorous training, and their howls would be a means of passing on commands received from riders. Soldiers who offer this explanation compare their organisation to that of a troop of trained horses, able to recognise signals given by their masters. They believe that a pack deprived of its leaders swiftly loses its ability to fight together. Some officers therefore hold that neutralising the riders is enough to turn Wargs into disorganised predators, whose reactions become comparable to those of natural wolves.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
Gondorians know Wargs as great malevolent wolves associated with Orcs and the wild lands of the North. Military accounts describe them as powerful animals, able to pursue Men over long distances and follow trails by means of their keen sense of smell. Their size allows some to serve as mounts, and their packs sometimes accompany Orcish warriors on raids. Soldiers' traditions stress their ability to move swiftly and attack several adversaries in concert. Their presence is known chiefly through accounts of military campaigns and testimony from travellers arriving from regions where these creatures are more frequent.

You know that Wargs possess an intelligence surpassing that of ordinary wolves and communicate in a language of their own. They can recognise the movements of a force, gather together, and pursue a common enterprise. Their alliance with the Orcs is ancient, but Wargs retain the ability to act without their riders. Gondorian traditions also distinguish them from the Werewolves mentioned in tales of the Elder Days, although the details of their origin are less well known. Their collective organisation explains why they are regarded as dangerous foes even when encountered far from Orcish forces.
outcomes.success:
The military traditions of Gondor preserve a developed knowledge of Wargs, passed down through chronicles, soldiers' accounts, and relations with the peoples of the northern regions. These creatures possess their own language, through which they exchange warnings, agree upon movements, and organise common enterprises. Their association with the Orcs rests upon an ancient alliance, sustained by shared interests and by their hostility towards the Free Peoples. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. Packs acknowledge their own leaders and can act independently of Orcish warriors.

Men familiar with these accounts know that Wargs are capable of observing a formation and recognising its weaknesses. Their speed enables them to follow a force on the march, while their intelligence leads them to seek passages where soldiers have less freedom of movement. A pack may scatter to test several approaches, then gather again when its members discover a favourable opportunity. Wargs may also break off an attack when confronted by unexpected resistance and alter their movements to exploit more advantageous ground. Military testimony stresses this adaptability, which distinguishes their behaviour from that of animals merely trained to fight.

Gondorian traditions also attach great importance to their autonomy. An Orc-band may be dispersed or defeated without the Wargs accompanying it immediately abandoning the region. Their organisation enables them to pursue their own purposes and rejoin others of their kind. Men knowledgeable about these creatures thus distinguish an encounter with a mounted troop from the threat posed by a pack acting on its own.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The deepest knowledge preserved among Gondorians distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves, from animals employed in war, and from the wolf-like creatures belonging to the oldest traditions of Middle-earth. Wargs possess an intelligence, a language, and an organisation that enable them to deliberate, acknowledge their leaders, and form alliances with Orcs while retaining their own will. Accounts depicting them as mere mounts fail to recognise this independence. Chronicles of the wars against the servants of the Shadow describe several kinds of wolf-like beings, but the best-preserved traditions distinguish their behaviour and the powers attributed to them. Among these creatures Wargs occupy a particular place through their corporeal nature, their ability to communicate, and their participation in organised military enterprises.

Men-at-arms acquainted with these traditions can compare the behaviour of a pack to that of a small force capable of planning its movements. Wargs observe opposing dispositions, recognise obstacles, and seek to exploit the opportunities offered by the terrain. They may follow the flanks of a column, divert an escort's attention, or separate a party of travellers before concentrating their attack. Their communications enable them to coordinate several movements without a rider constantly directing them. A retreat may be a calculated decision, and the dispersal of a pack may prepare its gathering elsewhere. These abilities explain their effectiveness as allies of the Orcs, but also the danger they pose when acting independently.

The oldest traditions sometimes associate their origin with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. They describe Wargs as descendants of a strain of wolves altered by an ancient curse, while other accounts speak of the Werewolves that served Morgoth, beings animated by evil spirits and belonging to a different nature. Gondorian scholars familiar with these tales distinguish traditions about Wargs from accounts of the supernatural powers of the Elder Days. Certain more obscure developments attribute a particular spiritual existence to Wargs themselves, but such beliefs belong to interpretations passed down through tradition rather than the ordinary observations of soldiers. Knowledge of their language, intelligence, and organisation remains the surest foundation for identifying them.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — Orcish breeding presented as their origin and a supposedly automatic reaction to military formations; failure — their autonomy is overlooked; successful results — military knowledge and historical distinctions. Accounts of corruption and spiritual nature are presented as traditions; their fuller elaboration comes from MERP/ICE, not from an explicit statement by Tolkien.
